Keep several answers alive, and let the whole sentence decide

Greedy picks one token per step and can never take it back. Beam search keeps the B best PARTIAL answers (beams) at once. Every step, each beam proposes its B most likely next tokens; all the proposals are ranked by the probability of the WHOLE sequence so far (a sum of log-probabilities); the best B
go on, and a proposal that ends with

A longer answer always has a lower raw score

H · Recap — greedy or beam search?
the two strategies side by side, and when to use which
The same model, two ways to read it
from the same decoder; they differ only in how many answers they keep alive while writing. Greedy keeps one; beam search keeps B. Everything else in the table follows from that.
the single most likely next token —
the B best of B × B candidates, ranked by the log-probability of the whole sequence
recoverable while the better path stays in the top B: "a" survived
as likely; greedy’s sentence was found too, and ranked last
B decoder rows, B top-k calls, a sort of B × B candidates
one row per sentence, only ever appended to
one row per beam — B times the memory — re-sorted every step by
set aside in completed; the search stops when it has B of them
keeps short answers from winning by default
many sentences at once (generate takes a batch)
one sentence at a time in this notebook (
repeats itself; locks in a bad first word
bland or overly generic text; too short without the penalty; with the notebook’s stopping rule it can stop before the longest answer finishes
the comparison and the cache check (
the model is confident — one token clearly leads at each step, so greedy and beam search agree
speed and memory matter: one decoder row per sentence, the smallest KV cache
you decode many sentences at once — evaluation over a whole validation set, as
the output is streamed token by token and must never be revised
there is one right answer and you want the most likely one: translation, summarisation — this
early words decide later ones, so a locally-best first word can lead astray, as "the" did here
you can afford about B times the work and the cache for each sentence
finished answers of different lengths must be compared fairly (the length penalty)
you want variety: open-ended or creative text, several different answers to the same input
deterministic search keeps repeating itself — for open-ended text, beam search tends toward bland,
keep it safe with temperature below
For the notebook’s task — a short summary with one right answer — beam search with
beams gives the better final answer, and the length penalty keeps it from stopping too early. Greedy stays the right tool for
: it is cheap, it batches, and on a well-trained, confident model the two often agree. When they disagree,

beam search usually returns the more likely sentence — but not always: greedy’s path can be pruned along the way, and the length penalty can deliberately prefer a longer answer with a lower raw probability, as it did in section C. Deep dive
adds the third option, top-k sampling, and does the arithmetic of all three on one row of
